extracted.intended_audience: mathematics faculty and researchers (prospective Ph.D. advisors, junior and mid‑career mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, career‑level guidance for mathematicians about directing Ph.D. students and managing research‑life activities (professional travel, sabbaticals, conferences, institute programs, outside offers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement to direct a Ph.D. thesis is a huge commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Agreeing to direct a student's Ph.D. thesis is a huge commitment. There are few other obligations in life that compare."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisor must take decision seriously because it entails a close, detailed relationship for 3–5 years, teaching how to conduct research, dealing with frustration and failure, and substantial time involvement. Don't accept lightly; get to know the student first through classes, reading courses, seminars, or departmental interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess student–advisor compatibility before agreeing
rubrics_metrics.description: "You really ought to get to know him/her first... you need to have some sense of whether this is a person with whom you are compatible, with whom you can communicate effectively, with whom you are comfortable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether you'll look forward to weekly meetings or dread them. If unsure, check the student's record in the Department Office, talk to colleagues, consult the Vice‑Chair for Graduate Studies and the Department Chair. Avoid students who 'bounce around' among advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor time commitment and meeting frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: "You will meet with the Ph.D. student at least once per week. And more frequently when things are hot or moving."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect regular weekly meetings and extra time during active phases; advisor must budget time accordingly and anticipate substantial mentoring and hand‑holding when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor responsibility for student's professional outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: "You will be largely responsible for getting this student a job if and when he/she finishes the program and earns the degree."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advising includes career mentoring and networking; successful advising can yield lifelong collaborations and friendships; advisors should actively help place students in positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh opportunity cost versus rewards of advising
rubrics_metrics.description: "Directing a Ph.D. thesis can certainly be one of the most rewarding features of academic life. But it can take a lot out of you. Some have argued that directing a Ph.D. thesis is giving up seven papers that one might have written."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the time cost (potentially reduced personal research output) but also that advising can produce new papers and be personally rewarding; factor this into decisions about taking students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate travel invitations based on funding and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Usually an invitation of this sort includes a promise to pay your travel expenses—hotel and airfare at the least. It could also include a per diem ... And it could include an honorarium. ... Some invitations ... will include no offer of subvention whatever."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before accepting invitations, confirm what is covered (airfare, hotel, per diem, honorarium). If no funding is offered, determine whether grant or departmental funds can cover costs. Consider the expectations (talks, participation) attached to the invitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate professional travel with personal plans when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: "One nice feature ... is that you can sometimes coordinate it with a personal trip. ... The professional part of the trip is still tax deductible and/or reimbursable; the personal part of the trip is of course 'on you.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, combine conferences with personal travel to maximize value; keep professional and personal expenses properly allocated for reimbursement/tax purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know differing institute funding models
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Banff covers room and board but not airfare; MSRI offers fixed stipends (often seed money); AIM covers travel, hotel, and per diem for one‑week workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarize yourself with the funding paradigms of institutes (Banff, MSRI, AIM, etc.) to plan travel and sabbaticals and to set realistic expectations about coverage and additional funding needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sabbatical as scholarly renewal and check institutional rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "The purpose of the sabbatical is to give the professor some time to recharge his/her batteries, to learn new things, to write a book or conduct a collaboration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand your institution's sabbatical policy (eligibility, pay arrangements, whether you must compete), plan sabbatical projects that demonstrate scholarly value, and use sabbatical time to develop research or collaborations. Note that adjuncts and many postdocs are typically ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sabbatical from leave of absence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Usually you take a leave when some other institution offers to pay your full—or at least a substantial amount of your—salary and benefits for the year or the semester."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaves are typically funded by the host institution and are negotiated differently from sabbaticals; be aware that multiple consecutive leaves may be restricted by administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prestige and host when justifying sabbaticals to administration
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was a surefire hit with the Dean if you told him you had arranged to spend a year at Harvard ... if instead you told the Dean that you wanted to spend the year at the University of Southeast Idaho to write a calculus textbook ... then he was less likely to be moved."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying for competitive sabbaticals at institutions where approval is discretionary, frame proposals to show scholarly benefit and, when appropriate, affiliation with highly regarded hosts to strengthen the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that your research 'clique' affects evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: "You will be judged ... in part by the crowd that you hang out with."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that field size and prominence influence how letters and committee evaluations are interpreted; working in a large, active field yields different visibility than a tiny niche. Strategize about research community and collaborations with this in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess your field's activity and standing using bibliographic/web tools
rubrics_metrics.description: "In today's electronic world ... anyone at all can get on MathSciNet and do a search ... Another Web search will tell immediately how many conferences there are in the subject area..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MathSciNet, web searches, conference listings, and speaker rosters to gauge activity level, key players, and visibility of your area; this helps put your work and career prospects in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conferences are for networking and finding problems (not just attending talks)
rubrics_metrics.description: "For me, going to conferences is to learn new problems to work on, and to establish new collaborations. For me, going to talks is an activity of definitely secondary interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize meeting people and forming collaborations; use breaks and social events for informal discussions. Develop a personal style for conferences (balance talks, working with collaborators, and social interaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference format and organization best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: "If it is well organized, then there will be plenty of breaks and a long lunch hour so that people have a chance to have private conversations ... The American Institute of Mathematics ... two expository talks each morning followed by a breakup into working groups in the afternoon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good conferences schedule breaks and opportunities for interaction; consider organizing formats (plenary + parallel sessions, working groups) that foster collaboration. When organizing, form a committee, apply for funding, create an invitation list, and consider publishing proceedings to impact the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICM role and talk types — know expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ICM is not like a working mathematics conference ... The plenary lectures ... one-hour talks ... invited talks ... 45 minutes ... uninvited talks ... twenty minutes or less."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ICM as a ceremonial, discipline‑defining event for exposure and community awareness; understand the three talk types and their purposes. Attend at least once for perspective on the field and its politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: January Joint Mathematics Meetings (JMM) — features and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: JMM is large, well attended, and covers a broad cross‑section of the profession; includes invited lectures, special sessions, panels, exhibits, and social events. Registration fees apply (about $200) but grants may be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use JMM for wide networking, meeting publishers, attending panels on professional topics, and seeing exhibits. Budget for registration, travel, and lodging; explore AMS grant support for attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling outside offers and negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: "If another institution values you, then it is quite likely that your home—University X—does not want to lose you... The home institution will not have to try as hard as the new invader..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect your home institution to counteroffer; weigh relocation costs, family considerations, spousal job assistance, and long‑term career benefits. Periodically reinventing yourself (changing jobs every 5–10 years) can be healthy professionally.
